title: Cloud Migration Planning Guide: How to Choose the Right Developer Tools Platform
description: Actionable cloud migration planning guidance covering implementation decisions, risk controls, practical tests, and a readiness checklist. Updated October 2026.
author: Marcus Rivera

sections.title: Build a dependency and workload inventory
sections.body: List applications, databases, scheduled jobs, identity systems, network dependencies, file storage, third-party integrations, and operational owners. For each workload, record business criticality, data classification, peak and normal usage, recovery needs, maintenance windows, and current operating cost. Identify undocumented dependencies before estimating a migration. A server list alone misses the queues, DNS records, credentials, certificates, batch jobs, and downstream consumers that can break after a move.

sections.title: Choose a migration pattern per workload
sections.body: Rehost can reduce immediate infrastructure change but may preserve inefficient architecture. Replatform changes selected managed services while limiting application rewrites. Refactoring can improve scalability or operations but carries more delivery risk and should have a clear business case. Retiring unused systems and retaining workloads that should not move can be valid decisions. Choose per application, document why, and avoid committing to one migration pattern for the entire estate.

sections.title: Model total cost and capacity
sections.body: Compare compute, storage, database, data transfer, backup, observability, support, security controls, licenses, and staff effort. Include migration tooling, temporary parallel-running environments, egress costs, and the cost of idle resources. Model a normal month and a peak month, then check how autoscaling, committed-use discounts, and regional requirements affect the result. Do not compare a cloud list price with an on-premises bill without accounting for what each figure includes.

sections.title: Design identity, network, and data controls
sections.body: Define account or subscription boundaries, least-privilege roles, service identities, network segmentation, secret storage, encryption, key ownership, and audit logging before moving production data. Confirm where data and backups will reside and who can access them. Test restore procedures, not just backup creation. Decide how traffic will be routed during cutover and how DNS, certificates, private connectivity, and external allowlists will be updated.

sections.title: Prove the migration with a pilot
sections.body: Choose a workload that is representative but recoverable. Rehearse provisioning from code, data transfer, application configuration, monitoring, backup restoration, and rollback. Compare latency, error rate, throughput, recovery time, and cost against the recorded baseline. Include realistic load and failure tests; a successful smoke test proves only that the happy path works. Record manual steps and eliminate or document them before scaling the migration.

sections.title: Plan data consistency and cutover
sections.body: Determine whether downtime is acceptable, whether changes must be replicated, and how data consistency will be verified. Define a freeze window or a controlled dual-write/replication approach only when the team understands its failure modes. Use checksums, row counts, application-level reconciliations, or domain-specific totals to confirm transferred data. Set a cutover decision owner, go/no-go criteria, user communication plan, and rollback deadline before the event begins.

sections.title: Operate and optimize after launch
sections.body: Assign ownership for alerts, incident response, patching, access reviews, cost budgets, service quotas, and recovery exercises. Tag resources consistently and alert on spend anomalies as well as technical failures. Review performance under real usage before rightsizing. Keep infrastructure definitions, deployment steps, and recovery instructions versioned so that a future rebuild does not depend on undocumented console changes.

sections.title: Migration readiness checklist
sections.body: Proceed only when dependencies are known, a target architecture and cost model are reviewed, data and identity controls are approved, the pilot meets acceptance criteria, recovery has been tested, and a named team can operate the service. Track remaining risks and exceptions. If the cloud move does not improve a defined business or operational outcome, pause and reassess rather than treating migration completion as the outcome itself.
